strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in RL benchmarking by providing the first comprehensive, systematically organized framework for evaluating memory capabilities across diverse scenarios
Well-motivated taxonomy of memory tasks grounded in cognitive science literature, organizing memory-intensive RL into four fundamental categories (Object, Spatial, Sequential, Memory Capacity)
Comprehensive dual benchmarks: MIKASA-Base systematizes ~30 existing environments while MIKASA-Robo introduces 32 carefully designed robotic manipulation tasks with clear progression in difficulty

Strong empirical validation demonstrating stark performance gaps between memory-less (PPO-MLP) and memory-enhanced (PPO-LSTM) agents, validating benchmark utility for distinguishing memory requirements
Practical implementation with Gymnasium API integration, provided code examples, and promise of open-source release enabling community adoption
Multiple observation modes (state, RGB, RGB+joints) and reward variants (dense/sparse) enabling flexible and realistic evaluation scenarios
Bridges abstract memory challenges and practical robotics applications, demonstrating real-world relevance beyond academic benchmarking
weaknesses: Limited agent architecture evaluation: restricted to PPO with MLP and LSTM backbones; missing evaluation of modern memory mechanisms (Transformers, attention, Neural Turing Machines, recent memory-augmented approaches)

Shallow analysis of memory mechanisms: paper shows memory matters but lacks investigation of how agents utilize memory, what patterns LSTMs learn, or which task categories benefit most from specific memory mechanisms

Incomplete experimental evaluation: no human baselines (especially for robotic tasks), limited sample efficiency analysis, no statistical significance testing, hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored, and no meta-learning/few-shot comparison

Limited novelty in individual components: MIKASA-Robo tasks are well-designed adaptations of existing robotic concepts; most base environments sourced from existing benchmarks (POPGym, DMLab-30); primary contribution is systematization rather than novel memory challenges

Insufficient task complexity analysis: no quantitative metrics for measuring memory-intensiveness; difficulty levels assigned arbitrarily without explicit, measurable criteria; lack of analysis on task distinctiveness and overlap in memory requirements

Limited architectural coverage of modern approaches: no evaluation of Transformers, attention mechanisms, or other state-of-the-art memory methods, severely limiting the benchmark's ability to drive progress on advanced memory mechanisms

Scope limitations: evaluation focused on partially observable settings and manipulation/navigation domains; missing exploration of continuous control, hierarchical memory, or compositional memory requirements

Incomplete comparisons and positioning: no comparison with other memory-focused evaluation frameworks, missing connection to cognitive science memory assessments, no comparison with meta-learning benchmarks that also require memory

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap in memory-enhanced RL research by providing a unified, standardized benchmark framework bridging fragmented evaluation approaches
Comprehensive framework combining diagnostic (MIKASA-Base) and complex robotic (MIKASA-Robo) tasks with well-articulated taxonomy of memory types grounded in cognitive science
Excellent documentation with detailed task descriptions, implementation details, code examples, and clear performance validation demonstrating genuine task difficulty
Well-designed robotic manipulation domain provides practical grounding and meaningful complexity beyond abstract benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily a benchmark curation effort rather than novel algorithms or techniques; tasks adapted from existing benchmarks and taxonomy relies on established cognitive science concepts

Severely incomplete baseline evaluation: only tests PPO-MLP and PPO-LSTM (dated methods); critically missing modern memory mechanisms (attention, graph networks, episodic memory, world models); lacks comparison with other memory benchmarks or their solution methods

Weak experimental validation: PPO-MLP achieving 100% success in state mode raises fundamental question whether tasks test memory or information access; dense rewards showing 100% success inadequately explained; minimal statistical reporting (no confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars on most results)

Disconnection between taxonomy and solutions: paper doesn't articulate which memory mechanisms should excel at which task categories; no evidence taxonomy captures fundamental difficulty dimensions; missing ablations on memory capacity, context length, and task properties

MIKASA-Robo task design concerns: artificially constrained tasks may not reflect organically important memory challenges in real-world robotics; limited justification for task selection; no comparison with established robotics benchmarks (LIBERO, MetaWorld)

Missing critical analysis of failure modes: no breakdown of why baselines fail; no ablation studies on task properties; no guidance on which architectural properties solve which tasks; analysis only confirms 'existing methods struggle' without explaining why

Insufficient scope and transferability: unclear whether insights generalize beyond tabletop manipulation; MIKASA-Base is purely diagnostic with limited novelty; no cross-domain validation or evidence of practical impact outside the benchmark

Reproducibility and statistical rigor gaps: no code available at review time; hyperparameter details for baseline training are sparse; some task specifications vague; learning curves lack explicit statistical tests; inadequate sample sizes for robust conclusions

strengths: Addresses a critical gap in RL benchmarking by providing the first comprehensive, unified framework for evaluating memory capabilities in agents
Well-grounded taxonomic classification framework based on cognitive science, organizing memory-intensive tasks into four fundamental types with principled structure
Comprehensive dual-pronged approach combining standardized evaluation (MIKASA-Base with 11 environments) and practical robotics-focused tasks (MIKASA-Robo with 32 carefully designed tasks)
Rigorous experimental validation demonstrating effectiveness: 100% success with full state info, clear memory requirements shown via RGB vs. state comparison and sparse reward experiments
Excellent presentation and reproducibility: clear writing, detailed implementation details, code examples, and comprehensive appendices enabling full reproducibility
Practical design grounded in realistic robotic manipulation scenarios (12 categories spanning touching, pushing, picking, rotating, intercepting) with clear relevance for real-world applications
Covers substantial breadth: 32 robotic tasks plus 11 existing environments with varying difficulty levels and reward structures
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—contribution is primarily in benchmarking organization rather than new memory mechanisms or RL algorithms
Narrow baseline evaluation using only PPO with MLP and LSTM backbones; missing evaluations of Transformers, attention mechanisms, episodic memory approaches, and specialized memory-augmented methods
Insufficient analysis of which memory mechanisms excel on different task types; limited transfer learning analysis across memory categories
Sparse reward analysis is incomplete; while Figure 9 shows some results, deeper investigation of how sparsity affects different memory types would strengthen claims
Missing comparative analysis with other memory-focused benchmarks or evaluation frameworks in the literature
Task difficulty calibration under-explored; limited systematic investigation of how task parameters affect learning across difficulty levels and memory types
No real-world validation or sim-to-real transfer analysis; limits practical applicability claims despite robotics focus
Minimal failure analysis and error investigation; could provide stronger guidance for practitioners on designing memory-enhanced architectures
Limited discussion of computational costs, scalability, sample efficiency, and training time across task types; no guidance for extending benchmark to new domains

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine fragmentation in memory-RL benchmarks
Systematic four-category classification framework grounded in cognitive science
Comprehensive scope with 32 robotic tasks, MIKASA-Base consolidation, and multiple evaluation modalities
Rigorous experimental validation with proper baselines and error reporting
Thorough documentation and implementation quality with promised code/dataset release
Clear task solvability validation (100% success in state mode)
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and future directions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: tasks are relatively straightforward applications of known memory concepts (color matching, ball interception, etc.)
Incomplete evaluation of modern memory mechanisms: focus on LSTM (2005) rather than recent approaches (S5, Mamba); only Decision Transformer tested among Transformers
Classification framework limitations: four categories map directly to established cognitive concepts; task categorization appears somewhat arbitrary with potential overlaps (e.g., TakeItBack-v0)
Sparse reward experimental concerns: near-zero offline RL performance (Table 6) makes discrimination difficult; no ablation on reward sparsity vs. difficulty scaling
VLA experiments limited to 5/32 tasks with insufficient fine-tuning, making conclusions about VLA memory capabilities unclear
Missing critical analyses: no systematic difficulty characterization, ablation studies on design choices, or inter-task correlation analysis
Task design realism concerns: most tasks are somewhat artificial; limited discussion of transfer to real-world scenarios
Reproducibility: code/datasets not available for review; some VLA hyperparameters underspecified

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap in RL—fragmented memory evaluation across studies with minimal overlap
Comprehensive benchmarking suite spanning online RL, offline RL, and VLA models across multiple training modes and reward settings
Systematic validation that tasks are solvable in state mode (100% SR) but challenging with visual observations, confirming benchmark efficacy
Well-organized taxonomy of memory types (Object/Spatial/Sequential/Capacity) grounded in cognitive science provides useful structure for systematic evaluation
Extensive documentation with implementation details, datasets, reproducibility information, and careful task descriptions across 32 robotic manipulation scenarios
weaknesses: Limited novelty: Primarily an engineering/benchmarking contribution without algorithmic or conceptual innovations; taxonomy borrowed from existing cognitive science literature

Problematic offline RL evaluation: Many methods achieve 0.00±0.00 success rate (Table 6), indicating potential unsuitability of benchmark or insufficient dataset diversity (only 1000 trajectories per task)
Weak VLA evaluation: Authors acknowledge 'limited fine-tuning due to computational constraints,' undermining this baseline section; conclusions about VLA memory capabilities unreliable

Shallow failure analysis: Documents that current methods struggle but provides minimal insight into why; lacks ablations on task difficulty factors and investigation of learning vs. computational bottlenecks

Scope limitations: All tasks confined to short-horizon tabletop manipulation (90-180 steps) in simulation; no truly long-term dependencies, meta-RL, or continual learning aspects despite their importance for memory
Taxonomy lacks empirical validation: No evidence that four memory types are sufficient or necessary; some tasks (e.g., RememberShapeAndColor) test multiple types simultaneously

Limited baseline sophistication: Evaluates standard methods (PPO, LSTM) but lacks advanced memory architectures (Neural Turing Machines, attention mechanisms, world models) or specialized memory RL algorithms
Confounding experimental design: RGB+joints mode combines visual learning with memory; joint state access provides unfair advantage; dense rewards unrealistic for real applications
Concurrent work diminishes novelty: MemoryBench (Fang et al. 2025) addresses similar problem space; paper dismisses it on task count but differentiation insufficient
Reproducibility gaps despite claims: Code link incomplete in abstract; heavy ManiSkill3 framework dependency introduces fragility; no significance testing between methods

strengths: Addresses a clear, well-documented gap in memory RL evaluation with Table 2 demonstrating fragmentation across papers
Comprehensive benchmark with 32 robotic tasks across 12 categories and well-motivated four-category memory taxonomy grounded in cognitive science
Exemplary reproducibility with open-source implementation, detailed appendices, code examples, and datasets for offline RL research
Thorough empirical validation across online RL (PPO, SAC, TD-MPC2), offline RL (DT, RATE, BC, CQL, DP), and VLA baselines with systematic difficulty progression
Clever validation methodology showing 100% success in state mode while demonstrating clear performance degradation in partial observability
Novel robotic task design directly addressing real-world challenges (occluded objects, multi-step memory-dependent procedures) not captured by existing benchmarks
Dual-benchmark approach (MIKASA-Base consolidating existing environments + MIKASA-Robo with new robotic tasks) providing both breadth and domain specificity
Well-written and clearly presented with effective visualizations and comprehensive experimental results
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: four-category taxonomy is intuitive but relatively straightforward; prior classification work exists (Ni et al., Yue et al., Cherepanov et al.), reducing originality
Narrow scope: all robotic tasks are simulated tabletop manipulation with simple objects; no sim-to-real transfer evaluation or exploration of complex manipulation scenarios
Primarily a benchmark contribution with no new algorithms or memory mechanisms proposed; may have limited perceived impact despite practical value
VLA experiments (Section 6.4) feel somewhat disconnected; limited fine-tuning (250 trajectories) constrained by computational resources weakens experimental comprehensiveness
Insufficient analysis of failure modes: many tasks show 0.00±0.00 success but paper doesn't deeply explain why methods fail or characterize specific missing memory capabilities
Task difficulty calibration unclear: how were complexity levels (3/5/9 colors, 3/5/7 items) chosen? No principled relationship between complexity and memory requirements formalized
Limited memory mechanism discussion: brief appendix survey of techniques (RNNs, SSMs, Transformers) but no guidance on which mechanisms suit different task types
Concurrent related work (Fang et al.'s MemoryBench) reduces uniqueness, though MIKASA-Robo is substantially more comprehensive (32 vs 3 tasks)
Generalization questions unaddressed: how do findings transfer to unseen task variations or other domains beyond tabletop manipulation?
Minor presentation issues: some figures difficult to parse (e.g., Figure 6 radar plot with overlapping lines); notation in Table 1 could be clearer
